progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: skills-s01 (reading routine, constraints), s02 (explain = cause and effect), s04 (verdict, criteria, evidence), s06 (trends with numbers); bio-m7-b09 (vaccination, memory cells, secondary response); bio-m7-b10 (herd immunity; hygiene breaks the contact link); chem-m7-c12 for drill 2 (facts given on the card). Students start Year 12.
progression.startsWith: A long question is marked as a whole, in bands. The video opens: The longest questions, worth six to nine marks, can decide a band. In six years of NESA's marking feedback for Chemistry and Biology, every report flagged answers that ignored the stimulus or copied it without explaining it, and more than half flagged judgements without reasons. So here's how to plan a long answer in a minute, build it one idea per paragraph, use the stimulus, and finish with a judgement when the verb asks.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining how bands work; unpacking a two-verb question with a constraint and a stimulus; writing a one-minute plan with the judgement first; building a PEEL paragraph that selects and interprets stimulus values; stating a judgement with its condition first and last; recognising why a weak answer sits in a lower band; planning an evaluate answer; rewriting a non-judgement as a judgement.
progression.nextLesson: Biology: evaluating disease control strategies (route bio-m7-g02, "Evaluate an infectious disease strategy"). In the "HSC exam skills" playlist: the subject-specific follow-ups (plan entry 9), root to name.

teaching.task: When a question is worth six to nine marks, how do you plan in about a minute, cover every demand with one idea per paragraph, use the stimulus as evidence, and end with a judgement that earns the top band?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the longest questions can decide a band, and recent marking feedback flags answers that ignore or copy the stimulus and judgements without reasons (1); (2) long answers are placed in a band by reading the whole answer, so the target is every demand covered with evidence and a supported judgement, not more words (2); (3) one HSC-style Biology measles question is set up for planning (3); (4) take it apart: two verbs, a constraint and the stimulus make four demands to tick (4); (5) plan in a minute: decide the judgement first, then one line per paragraph with the numbers it will use (5); (6) build each paragraph as point, evidence, explain and link (6); (7) the constraint needs one paragraph on immunity in the individual and one on the population (7); (8) using the stimulus means selecting and comparing values and saying what they mean, not copying the trend (8); (9) the judgement goes in the first line and comes back at the end with its reason and condition (9); (10) a weak and a strong answer side by side show the difference (10); two drills, one per subject, with feedback (11 to 14); decision rule (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the longest questions, worth six to nine marks, can decide a band, and NESA's marking feedback keeps flagging answers that ignore or copy the stimulus and judgements with no reasons. A marker places the whole answer in a band, so the target is every demand covered, with the stimulus used and a supported judgement, not more words. One HSC-style Biology question on measles vaccination and a school catch-up program is read and planned. Step one takes it apart into two verbs, a constraint and the stimulus, four demands to tick. Step two decides the judgement first, then jots one line per paragraph with the numbers it will use, in about a minute. Each paragraph is built as point, evidence, explain and link, with two paragraphs covering immunity in the individual and in the population. Using the stimulus means picking values, comparing them and saying what they mean, and the judgement opens the answer and returns at the end with its reason, here that cases were already falling before the program. A weak and a strong answer side by side show one verb against both, no numbers against selected values, and a bare verdict against a supported one. Two drills follow, a Biology plan and a Chemistry rewritten judgement, each with brief feedback, and a decision rule gathers unpack, decide, plan, PEEL and judge.
teaching.openingDecision: The longest questions, worth six to nine marks, can decide a band. In six years of NESA's marking feedback for Chemistry and Biology, every report flagged answers that ignored the stimulus or copied it without explaining it, and more than half flagged judgements without reasons. So here's how to plan a long answer in a minute, build it one idea per paragraph, use the stimulus, and finish with a judgement when the verb asks.
teaching.understandingCheck: "A hospital ward measured staff hand hygiene compliance and the rate of infections that patients caught on the ward. A hand hygiene training program began in July. In the same month, the ward also started a new daily cleaning routine. | | Jan to Jun (before) | Jul to Dec (after) | Hand hygiene compliance (%) | 45 | 82 | Infections caught on the ward (per 1,000 patient-days) | 6.0 | 2.5 | Evaluate the training program. (6 marks) Task: write a PLAN only: the demands, your judgement, and one line per paragraph." Model plan: demands: evaluate (judgement plus criteria), use the data, refer to how infections spread; judgement: "probably effective, but not proven by these data"; P1: hands carry pathogens between patients; hand hygiene breaks the contact link (b10); P2: compliance 45% → 82% while infections 6.0 → 2.5 (fewer than half); P3: the cleaning routine began in the same month, so the fall can't be credited to training alone; P4 (close): verdict with its condition (probably effective; a ward that trained without changing cleaning would show its effect). Crossed habit: "Start writing straight away" (no plan: the cleaning routine gets missed). card: "Evaluate the use of soap for washing clothes in a town with hard water. (5 marks)" with a student answer summarised in three body sentences (on the card): "Hard water contains Ca²⁺ ions, which react with soap to form insoluble calcium stearate (scum). This wastes soap and leaves grey deposits on fabric. Soap is made from renewable fats and breaks down readily in the environment." Her last line: "Overall, soap has advantages and disadvantages." Task: "Rewrite her last line so that it makes a judgement." Model line: "In this hard-water town, soap is a poor choice for washing clothes, because calcium ions turn much of it into scum, which wastes soap and leaves deposits on fabric, even though soap is renewable and breaks down readily." Crossed habit: "Overall, soap has advantages and disadvantages." (a summary, not a judgement). The card supplies every fact the line needs, so the drill tests only the judgement.
